items.sourceTitle: 24-Hour Economy targets 30,000 jobs with pharmaceutical park at Ningo Prampram …Today is deadline for drugmakers to register interest

source_propositions.source_text: The government has opened registration for pharmaceutical manufacturers to establish operations in the Legon Pharmaceutical Innovation Park (LePIP), a 2,000-acre facility planned at Ningo Prampram in the Greater Accra Region.

The project, being developed by the 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development (24H+) Authority with the Ghana Infrastructure and Investment Fund (GIIF), is expected to create wealth and an estimated 30,000 jobs, according to the Authority.
Companies have until on October 12, 2026 to submit expressions of interest.
About 70 per cent of Ghana’s pharmaceutical demand is met through imports, costing the country more than $300 million annually, the call for expressions of interest says.
The government has set a target of replacing 50 per cent of imports with locally produced medicines by 2030.
The Authority describes LePIP as Ghana’s first integrated pharmaceutical innovation park, designed to make the country a manufacturing and export hub for West Africa and beyond.

Under the plan, a special purpose vehicle will provide shared infrastructure, including power, water and steam meeting Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards, an effluent treatment plant, cold-chain warehousing and ready-built factory shells.
Quality control laboratories, supervised by the University of Ghana, and a research centre focused on tropical diseases will also be provided.
Tenants will pay fees or lease charges for these services.
Companies producing active pharmaceutical ingredients, generics, vaccines, herbal medicines and diagnostics are eligible.
Joint ventures and consortia may apply.
Anchor tenants may be offered equity in the special purpose vehicle, subject to final terms.

The bank said the transaction was arranged in coordination with a major US bank, which it did not name, opening a channel to finance oil imports and settle payments through the formal banking system.The move marks a step toward restoring Syria's access to international banking channels following the removal of US sanctions and its designation as a state sponsor of terrorism.Saudi Arabia's energy minister signed three memorandums of understanding with Kuwait, Qatar and Egypt to strengthen energy cooperation, the Saudi state news agency said on Sunday.The agreement with Qatar sets a framework for collaboration in petroleum, natural gas and petrochemicals, including exploring joint opportunities to develop pipelines for transport and exports.Syria no longer classified as state sponsor of terrorismThe United States officially removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism at the end of August.

"There is no longer any obstacle to investment, doing business and rebuilding economic life in Syria," he said.“ These actions were all taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed Al-Sharaa to fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.Syria had been on the list since 1979, when Washington accused the government of former President Hafez al-Assad of supporting militant groups.
The designation remained throughout the rule of his son Bashar Al-Assad, who was toppled by rebels led by current President Ahmed Al-Sharaa in December 2024.

11 (SANA) A landmark financial transaction was completed Sunday as Syria’s central banking authority issued its first letter of credit (LC) through a major U.S. financial institution in 14 years, backing a strategic oil import agreement.

The Central Bank of Syria confirmed in an official statement that the banking mechanism was established for the Syrian Petroleum Company to execute a commercial deal with Saudi Aramco, opening a direct channel for energy deliveries to the local market.

The central bank emphasized that the transaction marks a critical shift toward re-establishing official banking channels for strategic trade, establishing a reliable settlement and financing structure for national fuel imports.
The announcement follows high-level financial discussions in New York on October 5, where Central Bank Governor Safwan Raslan met with officials from the U.S.
Federal Reserve Bank to discuss practical operations and account management between the two institutions.

items.sourceTitle: Roman fort found in Wales could prove myth of emperor’s camp is real

source_propositions.source_text: Exclusive: Finds suggest account in medieval folklore of a camp near Frenni Fawr hill was rooted in reality Magnus Maximus, the Roman emperor who ruled Britain in the fourth century, led his troops against the Picts and Scots, but a theory that he also established a military camp near Frenni Fawr hill in Wales has so far been based on folklore.
Now fourth-century coins, among other finds at a newly identified Roman fort in Pembrokeshire, suggest the medieval tale was rooted in reality, to the excitement of archaeologists.

The fort was discovered by Dr Mark Merrony, a leading Roman specialist at the University of Oxford. He heads an excavation that is bringing to life a story about Magnus Maximus, as told in the Mabinogion, a collection of medieval epic tales of myth, magic and miracles.
Merrony expressed excitement that this landscape held the only Roman military site close to where the Mabinogion places the emperor.
“If Magnus Maximus was there, there must have been an army there,” he said.

“It’s such a remote area but the tale mentions the easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills, which is where this site is. The presence of a heavily fortified Roman auxiliary fort may help unlock the mystery of a Mabinogion legend that has endured for nearly 1,700 years.”

In The Dream of Macsen Wledig , medieval storytellers used the emperor’s name in Welsh in recounting his rise to power. They described how on his military manoeuvres, he pitched his camp at Frenni Fawr, the 395-metre (1,300ft) easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills.
There had been no archaeological evidence for a Roman marching camp or fort on the summit of the Frenni Fawr or below it until now.
Merrony discovered it about 2 miles (3.5km) south-west of the summit in 2024.
Satellite imagery had shown a convincing outline in an overgrown field and, shortly after visiting it, his eye was caught by a Roman tile, which turned out to be the first of many.

International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that artificial intelligence was hitting the global labor market like a "slow-moving tsunami," with young graduates first in line to be knocked down.
"People to worry about, first and foremost, [are] young people that are coming into the labor market," Georgieva said at a panels on Monday.

"Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks. But if they're gone, I don't think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as ... professional future."

Speaking on the same panel, Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who co-chairs the World Bank's Jobs Council, called for governments to make "crisis-era" support measures a permanent tool for getting young people into work.

What governments did during the Covid-19 pandemic and, in some cases, the global financial crisis "now has to be thought of not as a crisis measure, but as part of the structural, the menu of structural policies," he said.

That means working with the private sector, and incentivizing firms to hire fresh graduates, because "the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," Shanmugaratnam said.

The remarks show that policymakers are moving from debating whether AI will disrupt jobs to deciding how to cushion the fallout, at a time when rapidly aging populations, particularly in Asia, already threaten to shrink workforces.

World Bank President Ajay Banga, estimates 1.2 billion young people will turn 18 over the next 15 years, and the private sector, which already generates 75% to 85% of jobs in any country, will have to absorb most of them.

Governments' role is to make that possible, he said, by building infrastructure, setting policy and "de-risking" private capital, or lowering the risks that deter investors from putting in money at scale.
"It is private capital that creates jobs," he said.
The IMF estimates that about 40% of jobs worldwide will eventually be "augmented, downgraded or eliminated."

The technology is already reducing demand for many human workers by taking over routine, repetitive tasks, she said THE head of the International Monetary Fund has warned of the disruptive threat from artificial intelligence to the labor market and taxation, urging policymakers to rethink education and act now to help society adapt.

“It is a slow-moving tsunami, but tsunami none the less,” Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said on Monday (Oct 12) during her first appearance at the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok.
Speaking at a session on AI’s impact on employment, she said the technology is already hollowing out demand for many human workers by taking over routine, repetitive tasks.

At the same time, it’s increasing low-paying jobs in sectors like construction, which she said is “not a story to celebrate.” It’s a transformation with far-reaching consequences for public finances, Georgieva said.
The risk is that AI strains government revenues by tilting the economy toward capital and away from labour — traditionally the main source of tax income.
The comments are the latest warning about the potential shock from AI on jobs and the global economy.
Young workers in AI-exposed fields have already seen a slowdown in hiring, leaving new entry-level applicants far more vulnerable.
Concern is also growing that the technology will widen inequality, with its gains so far concentrated among a narrow set of workers and economies despite a global investment supercycle.
Five decades of milestones and moments that shaped Singapore’s success story - told through our headlines.
“We cannot today imagine what exactly the world of work will be five years from now,” she said.
“But we can be disciplined and carefully assess what is happening, and then draw lessons, but — most importantly — act on them now.”
Despite the employment headwinds, the technology can ultimately prove a positive for growth overall.
The IMF estimates the spread of AI can add up to a percentage point to growth in advanced Asian economies.
Such a growth boost “is a very big deal,” Georgieva said, adding it will “more than offset” the drag from aging in rich countries across the region.

Artificial intelligence (AI) could create new jobs, raise productivity and accelerate economic growth in developing countries, global economic leaders told delegates at the 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group in Bangkok on Monday (October 12).

At the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center, World Bank Group President Ajay Banga, Singapore’s President Tharman Shanmugaratnam and IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva discussed how affordable, practical AI tools could benefit farmers, healthcare workers, businesses and entrepreneurs. Their session, “Small AI: More and Better Jobs”, focused on technology suited to the needs and resources of developing economies.
Georgieva explained that surging investment in AI infrastructure was helping sustain global economic growth at around 3%, despite the energy supply shock.

The expansion has particularly benefited Asian suppliers of AI hardware and infrastructure, including Thailand. She estimated that the investment boom could add 0.5 to 1 percentage point to growth in advanced Asian economies and 0.2 to 0.8 percentage point in emerging Asian economies.
These gains could also help offset the economic drag from ageing populations.
While the first wave of AI spending has largely involved infrastructure, Georgieva expected wider adoption to deliver the next major gains.
“The next wave of AI would be adoption. And there everybody can participate,” she told the gathering.
However, she stressed that developing economies needed reliable electricity, digital infrastructure, skilled workers and safeguards against misuse to realise the technology’s potential.

Banga warned that approximately 1.2 billion young people would turn 18 over the next 15 years, making the creation of meaningful employment a development priority. He argued that public investment in schools, healthcare, transport and training should be viewed through the lens of job creation.
While governments could create the conditions for investment, private businesses would remain the main source of employment.

“It is private capital that creates jobs. Governments enable,” Banga explained, adding that the private sector generates between 75% and 85% of jobs. He identified three conditions needed to attract investment: strong physical and human infrastructure, transparent governance and business-friendly policies, and government support to manage risks that deter private investors.

Banga highlighted five areas with strong potential for job creation: infrastructure, smallholder agriculture, primary healthcare, tourism and value-added manufacturing. He pointed to Thailand’s tourism sector as an example of opportunities for further job creation. He argued that affordable “small AI” applications, rather than relying exclusively on expensive, advanced AI systems, could deliver practical benefits in developing economies.

items.sourceTitle: Intensive breathwork reduces brain blood flow and alters neural communication

source_propositions.source_text: Intensive breathing exercises can reduce blood flow to the brain by up to 45% and alter communication between brain networks, according to a new brain-imaging study.
Participants reported experiences resembling some effects of psychedelic drugs, including altered perception, vivid mental imagery, a sense of unity and changes in self-experience.
The researchers, presenting the work at the ECNP Congress in Munich, say changes in brain communication, rather than reduced blood flow alone, appear to be key to the altered state.
The study involved 30 healthy, experienced breathwork practitioners who performed high-ventilation breathwork during MRI scanning.

Participants reported strong altered states of consciousness, describing a predominantly oceanic state – in other words, a deep feeling of connection to the universe - resembling that of a moderate to high dose of LSD or psilocybin, albeit with less pronounced visual effects.
Brain imaging showed that global grey-matter cerebral blood flow fell by around 45% during the session, on average from 16.24 to 9.81 ml/100g/min.
Those who reported stronger altered states also showed greater changes in the brain's default mode network, which is involved in self-reflection and self-related thinking.
The researchers suggest that the intensity of the experience is not simply explained by reduced blood flow.
Instead, the experience might track more closely with changes in communication within the default mode network, a brain system linked to self-reflection and self-related thought.

Lead researcher Dr Christian Schmitz, Central Institute of Mental Health, Mannheim in Germany, said: " Many people who practice intensive breathwork report profound changes in perception and self-experience, yet the underlying brain mechanisms remain poorly understood. Our study suggests that these experiences are linked not only to marked changes in cerebral blood flow, but also to alterations in how key brain networks communicate".

'Co-Coordinator, Hana Adolphi said, " Breathwork is a legal, inexpensive and non-pharmacological intervention that may provide a valuable tool for studying altered states of consciousness. Understanding these mechanisms could also help inform future research into novel approaches for mental health treatment. Nevertheless, this was a relatively small study, and the findings should be considered preliminary. Larger studies will be needed to determine whether these brain changes have clinical relevance."

Commenting, Dr Guy Fincham (Brighton and Sussex Medical School, UK) said: "This study is intriguing as it is starting to extend findings from recent breathwork research that intensive breathing practices may yield altered states of consciousness which individuals describe in ways analogous to psychedelic compounds, and under brain-imaging conditions. These findings are important because such altered subjective experiences may be harnessed for the improvement of mental health, and an accessible non-pharmacological route such a breathwork could prove invaluable for many. We should note that the study was uncontrolled and the sample was made up of experienced practitioners, so replication of this in breathwork-naïve participants using a randomised-controlled design will help determine whether these findings can translate more widely and produce therapeutic benefit".
